It describes that school principal questionnaire responses are weighted so that they are proportionate to the number of 15-year-olds enrolled in each school, indicating the use of complex survey weighting for school-level reporting. For student performance indicators (e.g., mean scores and proficiency-level shares), the report relies on PISA’s international sampling and scaling framework; however, the excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable names or replicate-weight procedures. Because this is a descriptive large-scale assessment report (not an ML modeling paper), the appropriate weights are those used in the underlying PISA results volumes and technical documentation; analysts should follow the PISA 2009 technical report and the PISA results volumes for the exact weighting and variance estimation approach.

data.outcome_summary: PISA 2009 at a Glance summarizes results from the OECD Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) 2009, focusing primarily on reading, with updated assessments in mathematics and science. The target population is 15-year-olds (15y3m–16y2m) who have completed at least 6 years of formal schooling, sampled across 65 participating countries and economies (with additional partner coverage assessed in a second round). The report presents proficiency-level distributions (e.g., shares below Level 2 and at Levels 5–6) and mean score comparisons, and it highlights statistically significant differences only. It also reports equity-related associations (e.g., socio-economic background and reading performance) and learning-to-learn correlates (e.g., reading enjoyment and strategy awareness), while providing definitions of proficiency levels and OECD averaging conventions. The excerpt does not provide explicit PV or missing-data handling procedures for the at-a-glance analyses, which are instead documented in the underlying PISA results volumes and technical report.
